title: Why Is There Pressure, and What To Do About It
author: Leading in Product
source: Leading in Product on Substack, December 16, 2025
summary: The author argues that crushing pressure is not inherent to leadership but a symptom of changeable organisational patterns. Unclear direction turns small decisions into battles, trust gaps trigger oversight layers that justify still more oversight, information anxiety drives meeting overload, and over-centralisation creates bottlenecks. The fixes are practical: clarity through written strategy, trust through radical transparency, information rhythms that replace ad-hoc meetings, and pushing decision-making down through written criteria. The reframe is decisive: the most effective leaders are not those who thrive under pressure but those who build organisations where good work happens without it. Shifting from managing pressure to reducing its source is more demanding than heroic strain and more lasting; it names ambient stress as a design problem, not a personal one, and design problems are solvable.
points: Four organisational patterns (unclear direction, trust gaps, information anxiety, over-centralisation) produce pressure that can be named and changed through design, not managed through willpower.
Clarity up front reduces the need for people to hunt guidance; transparency replaces ad-hoc meetings; decision criteria push authority down and reduce leadership bottlenecks.
The most effective leaders build organisations where good work happens without constant pressure, shifting the work from managing strain to designing its source away.
quotes: We’ve all been there. That crushing feeling of being squeezed from every direction. Stakeholders want faster delivery. Teams are confused about priorities. Leadership keeps asking for more updates while we’re already drowning in meetings.
Much of the pressure we feel comes from organizational patterns that we can actually change.

When direction is unclear, everything becomes a battle. Without clear direction, teams can’t move quickly because they’re constantly second-guessing themselves. This uncertainty creates bottlenecks everywhere.” “When trust is missing, organizations panic. They create layers of approval. Extra oversight. More checks and balances. This creates a vicious cycle. The lack of trust makes teams less effective, which then justifies even more oversight.

People schedule meetings because they’re scared. Scared of missing something important. Scared they don’t have enough information to do their jobs properly. Before you know it, your calendar is packed.

Build trust through radical transparency. Share your planning process openly. When problems arise, bring them up before others discover them. Admitting problems early makes people trust you more, not less.

Push decision-making down. Create frameworks. Write down decision criteria. Give your team the tools to make good choices without checking with you first. The goal isn’t losing control. It’s creating systems that work even when you’re not directly involved.

The most effective product leaders aren’t those who thrive under constant pressure. They’re the ones who build organizations where good work can happen without that pressure in the first place.” Archived from Leading in Product on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
